law: A step is done when it has a link. The spine is the mission. Publish waits for a receipt.

nodes.title: Welcome
nodes.evidence: A short public note (gist or Google Doc) with two things: the board rule in your own words, and which two open steps you will work on this week.
nodes.why: Watch, then write one short note. That is the whole first step.
nodes.reading: This page is the written lesson. The film is on this page too.
nodes.reviewFor: the rule said plainly, with no appeal to effort or hours, plus two steps that can run in the same week because nothing connects them on the map.

tasks.title: Write the rule in your own words
tasks.done_when: Your note has one or two sentences, in your words, explaining when a step lights and why that rule exists.
how: Open a gist or a Google Doc. Write the rule the way you would explain it to a friend.
If your sentence mentions effort or time spent, rewrite it. Keep both answers in the same note.

tasks.title: Name two steps you can run this week
tasks.done_when: The same note names It runs and The four skills (or any two open steps with no line between them), plus one sentence on how you will split the week.
how: Default pair while both are open: It runs (boot the desk) and The four skills (write the skill names with examples). Look at the map: no connecting line means they are independent.
One URL lights this step. Paste it under Turn this in when you are ready.

nodes.title: It runs
nodes.evidence: A link anyone can open that shows the desk status output after you cloned studio/ and ran the two README commands.
nodes.why: Before you can learn from a system, it has to run on your machine. This step hands you the desk and gets it breathing.
nodes.reading: Everything you need is inside the studio repo you receive at kickoff: its README lists the two boot commands, and MISSION.md (explained below) is your assignment brief.
nodes.reviewFor: a stranger can follow the link and see the inherited system actually running.

tasks.title: Boot Northline Desk on your machine
tasks.done_when: The test command reports green, and `python3 -m northline status` prints the queue: four tickets, one of them T-1842 sitting on Support.
how: Both commands are in studio/README.md. Run them from the studio/ folder in a fresh terminal. If something fails, the error is the lesson; read it before you search it.

tasks.title: Save the proof it ran
tasks.done_when: The status output is pasted at a public link (a GitHub gist works).
how: The output must show T-1842 on Support. That line is the setup for the next four nodes.

nodes.title: The four skills
nodes.evidence: A one-page note: the four skills in your words, with one honest example each from work you have already done.
nodes.why: Every review here uses four named skills. Learn the names calmly now, before a review uses them about your work.
nodes.reading: The four are explained below. Your evidence is the four skills in your own words.
nodes.reviewFor: each skill in your words, plus one example from work you have already done, including a time you lacked the skill.

tasks.title: Write the four in your words
tasks.done_when: Each skill has one sentence and one example from your work.
how: Template: for each skill, one sentence in your words, then one example from work you have already done. Include at least one miss.

tasks.title: Save the note
tasks.done_when: Anyone can open the link (gist or doc) and read all four skills with your examples.
how: Paste a public gist or doc URL, somewhere a stranger can read the text.

nodes.title: You can read a system
nodes.evidence: A note that follows ticket T-1842 from the incoming file to the stored team, and names three files a change would break.
nodes.why: The job is inherited systems: code that existed before you arrived. If you cannot redraw a path from memory, you have not understood it yet.
nodes.reading: MISSION.md in the studio repo is your assignment brief. This lesson explains the tracing method; the brief tells you what's at stake.
nodes.reviewFor: a map drawn before any assistant, naming three files a change would break.

tasks.title: Trace T-1842
tasks.done_when: You can redraw T-1842's full path, incoming note, through each function, to the stored team, from memory, without the code open.
how: Read in the data's order, not the file order. Start where a note enters the system and follow the calls. Paper beats screen here; redrawing is a test of memory, not art.

tasks.title: Save the trace
tasks.done_when: A public note or gist names the path, the wrong turn for T-1842, and three files a fix would touch.
how: One URL. Paper photo is fine if the writing is readable.

video.title: Reading code you did not write

nodes.title: You change messy code
nodes.evidence: A pull request on studio/ that includes your engineering contract, failure log, and agent log.
nodes.why: This is the center of the mission: one deliberate change to messy code, done with professional ceremony. Portfolios of greenfield toys all look alike; a defended change to inherited work does not.
nodes.reading: CHANGE-MENU.md in the studio repo offers three changes: A (fix the routing: the mission), B (a reporting feature: allowed only after A), C (rewrite the SLA engine: a deliberate trap). This lesson explains the ceremony; the menu explains the choice. Short reading: Humans around the queue (who owns done).
nodes.reviewFor: Change A, a written refusal of trap C, a contract accepted before the diff, and both logs.

tasks.title: Name the humans around the ticket
tasks.done_when: Your note names who filed it, who it was sent to, who should have owned it, and what that owner would call done.
how: Write this before the contract. If you cannot name them, you do not yet know what the change is for.

tasks.title: Write the contract, then change
tasks.done_when: Your PR is open on the studio repo with all three documents in it: the accepted contract, the failure log, and the agent log.
how: Do not tidy the repo to make the lesson prettier.

tasks.title: Save the PR
tasks.done_when: The URL is the PR.
how: Submit it.

video.title: Working inside code you did not write

nodes.title: You can prove it
nodes.evidence: A test or command that fails while T-1842 sits on Support, and passes when it sits on Billing.
nodes.why: The desk's tests can pass while a customer sits in the wrong queue. This step teaches the difference between a test that exists and a check that would catch a real lie.
nodes.reading: Open tests/test_routing_happy.py in the studio repo. Your job is the test that would have caught it. Optional brief: Verification tax.
nodes.reviewFor: a check that fails when the ticket is misrouted, and that a stranger can run from your link.

tasks.title: Write the stranger-runnable check
tasks.done_when: One command anyone can run. You watched it fail before the fix and pass after.
how: Don't delete the happy-path test. Add the one that tells the truth beside it.

tasks.title: Save the check
tasks.done_when: The link is the test file or the command output.
how: Repo file on the PR.

nodes.title: Someone else marked it up
nodes.evidence: The review thread URL, showing another person marked up the work.
nodes.why: Solo work is unverified work. Teams hire people who can ask for a review, absorb it, and answer without flinching.
nodes.reading: The request format is in the lesson. The reviewer is arranged through the cohort; you don't need to find one.
nodes.reviewFor: how you asked, and how you answered: selective agreement, not a blanket yes.

tasks.title: Ask for the review properly
tasks.done_when: The request names what to look at and what you are unsure about.
how: Template: look at <file or lines> · I am unsure about <risk>. Do not make them find the risk.

tasks.title: Save the thread
tasks.done_when: The thread shows another person's marks.
how: Submit the URL.

video.title: Send work, get notes, change it

nodes.title: You defend it live
nodes.evidence: An unlisted recording of your defense, plus the filled external-reader form.
nodes.why: Eight minutes on camera defending your change to an engineer who did not help you. This is the strongest single artifact the program produces.
nodes.reading: The six defense questions and the external-reader form live in the studio repo under evidence/. Read both before you record; there are no surprise questions.
nodes.reviewFor: you own the change live. The recording and the external form are both at the link.

tasks.title: Record the eight minutes
tasks.done_when: You answer the six defense questions without inventing detail.
how: Record unlisted. Answer the six defense questions without inventing detail you cannot show.

tasks.title: Get one external verdict
tasks.done_when: A working engineer who did not help you filled the form.
how: studio/evidence/external-reader.md

tasks.title: Save recording and form
tasks.done_when: One URL that opens both, or two URLs in one note.
how: Submit it.

nodes.title: A stranger can find the work
nodes.evidence: One profile line or post that links your defense recording (or the PR pack the defense walks), published only after that receipt exists.
nodes.why: Work a stranger cannot find might as well not exist. The trail points at the defense you already earned.
nodes.reading: One post or one profile line that points at real work is the entire scope.
nodes.reviewFor: the trail points at the defense or the PR the defense covers, and it went up after that receipt existed.

tasks.title: Publish one trail that points at the work
tasks.done_when: Anyone can go from the post or profile to the defense recording or the PR the defense walks.
how: One live post or profile line with a clickable URL to the defense or the PR pack it covers.

tasks.title: Save that URL
tasks.done_when: The link opens the post or the live profile line that points at the defense or that PR.
how: Submit the public URL once the post is live.

nodes.title: The world runs on your machine
nodes.evidence: a gist with the outputs of the onboarding doc's current verification steps, plus a screenshot of your avatar standing in your locally-running world.
nodes.why: Before you can change a live system you must be able to run it: the same code, started the same way production starts it, on your own machine.
nodes.reading: ONBOARDING.md in the world server repo is the living setup doc. It always reflects the world's current state; when the world changes, it changes. Follow the live doc.
nodes.reviewFor: Both boot paths ran, and you can say what is different about them.

tasks.title: Run the world server, both ways
tasks.done_when: The server runs in dev mode AND under Docker, and you completed every verification step the onboarding doc currently lists.
how: ONBOARDING.md walks it command by command. If a step fails, the error is the lesson; 30 honest minutes, then #asks.

tasks.title: Compare dev mode to production mode
tasks.done_when: Your gist shows the same endpoint answering in both modes, with one sentence on why any difference exists.
how: The difference, or its absence, is the week-1 systems lesson.

tasks.title: Walk into your own world
tasks.done_when: A public image or gist shows two browser tabs, two avatars, on your local world. That URL is the evidence.
how: Point the web client at your local server; the onboarding doc shows how.
Screenshot both tabs, upload to a gist or image host, paste the link.

video.title: A live game server on your laptop

nodes.title: Your first world ticket
nodes.evidence: a merged pull request on the world server repo, containing the engineering contract, the failure log, and the agent log.
nodes.why: You take a ticket from the project board and ship it into the live world with full professional ceremony.
nodes.reading: The board is the open issues on the gridschool-world-server repo. You get your ticket in the Monday call's sprint planning: or message Aden any time you're ready for one.
nodes.reviewFor: A half-page map before the diff, then a PR with full ceremony.

tasks.title: Take a ticket in sprint planning
tasks.done_when: A ticket from the current board is assigned to you, with its points and done-when read aloud in the Monday call.
how: Pick small. One finished small ticket with full ceremony beats a half-done ambitious one every time.

tasks.title: Map before you touch
tasks.done_when: A written half-page: what the ticket touches, what calls it, what could break.
how: If your nanograph already parses this repo's language (graph track, seam node), use it here, that is why you're building it.

tasks.title: Ship it with full ceremony
tasks.done_when: CI green, contract + failure log + agent log complete, review requested, and the ticket's own done-when satisfied.
how: The PR template is the checklist.

nodes.title: Staging to live, your hands on the wheel
nodes.evidence: the deploy run URL you drove, and the health check you watched go green on the real domain.
nodes.why: Most bootcamp grads have never deployed anything anyone uses. You will have promoted a live multiplayer world with your change in it, on camera, with me beside you.
nodes.reading: The Friday promote session. Merge deploys staging automatically; live is a decision, and this week it is yours to execute.
nodes.reviewFor: You drove the promote, and the deploy note a stranger can open says what changed.

tasks.title: Drive the promote
tasks.done_when: Your ticket's image is serving on the world URL and /health answers over TLS.
how: Group session. You share the screen, not me.

tasks.title: Write the deploy note
tasks.done_when: Five lines in #world: what shipped, how you verified, what you'd watch overnight.
how: The note is the habit; ops teams live on these.

nodes.title: A feature wearing your mark
nodes.evidence: your feature visible at play.gridschool.org with its maker's mark, and the PR that shipped it.
nodes.why: Anyone can say they built something. Your friends and family can walk into this one.
nodes.reading: Maker's marks are the only in-world credit. The world renders no progress bars: the thing itself is the proof.
nodes.coming: Opens when the web client is published at play.gridschool.org. The server-side path (ticket, deploy) is live now.

tasks.title: Ship a visible feature
tasks.done_when: A stranger at play.gridschool.org can see or use it without being told where to look.
how: Feature issues (GF-F1, GF-F2) or an earned proposal.

nodes.title: Source code is data
nodes.evidence: a repo where nanograph parses itself, plus graph.json generated from a real project you did not write.
nodes.why: Comprehension made executable. Every question you will ever ask about a codebase, who calls this, what breaks, starts with the graph you build here.
nodes.reading: Three text modules. Type the code. Do not paste it.
nodes.reviewFor: nanograph.py parses itself, the nested-function bug is fixed, and graph.json exists for a repo you did not write.

tasks.title: Modules 00-01: the parser parses itself
tasks.done_when: nanograph.py reports its own functions and calls, and you fixed the nested-function bug from the exercise.
how: Python stdlib ast. Nothing to install.

tasks.title: Module 02: edges across files
tasks.done_when: graph.json exists for a real repo, and you committed the ambiguity confession from the exercise.
how: Two passes: collect definitions, then resolve calls.

nodes.title: Who calls what
nodes.evidence: CLI output of callers, callees, and a --hops blast radius on a repo you care about, committed to the README.
nodes.why: “If I change this, what breaks?” answered in milliseconds instead of an afternoon. This is the question interviews actually probe.
nodes.reading: Modules 03-04. Type the code. One dial: --hops.
nodes.reviewFor: callers, callees, and a --hops blast radius on a repo you care about, in the README.

tasks.title: callers / callees commands
tasks.done_when: nanograph callers <fn> answers from graph.json without re-parsing.
how: Build the reverse index once; queries are lookups.

tasks.title: Blast radius with --hops
tasks.done_when: Reverse BFS matches the paper drawing you made in module 00, or you can explain the difference.
how: Your hand-drawn graph from episode 00 is the test fixture.

nodes.title: Cycles, rank, coupling
nodes.evidence: a findings write-up with numbers: one real cycle, the top five load-bearing functions, the worst-coupled module pair.
nodes.why: Architecture stops being an opinion when you can measure it. PageRank on a call graph finds the code everyone leans on.
nodes.reading: Modules 05-07. PageRank is repeated averaging; no math beyond fractions.
nodes.reviewFor: A findings write-up that reads like a review comment, not a data dump.

tasks.title: Find real cycles
tasks.done_when: nanograph cycles names at least one true cycle in a real repo, and you explain why it matters or doesn't.
how: DFS with a stack. Module 05 walks it.

tasks.title: Rank + coupling with numbers
tasks.done_when: A note or PR comment in your nanograph repo ranks load-bearing symbols with numbers, in code-review tone, not a raw dump.
how: Degree first, then PageRank. Modules 06-07 open under this step.
Commit the write-up next to graph.json, or paste a gist URL that quotes the numbers.

nodes.title: Swap the parser, keep the graph
nodes.evidence: your same queries running on the world server's C#: the map you make of it goes into your next world ticket.
nodes.why: The graph never knew who parsed it. That seam is the deepest lesson in the series, and the moment your tool and the game connect: you map the live world with the thing you built.
nodes.reading: Module 08. tree-sitter behind the same interface; then map the world server.
nodes.reviewFor: The same graph interface, a second language, and a blast radius on the world server.

tasks.title: tree-sitter behind the same interface
tasks.done_when: graph.json builds from a non-Python repo with zero changes to the query code.
how: The parser is a plugin; the graph is the contract.

tasks.title: Map the world server
tasks.done_when: Blast radius of the function your next world ticket touches, posted in #world.
how: This artifact feeds wd.ticket's map-before-you-touch task.

nodes.title: Feed the model less, get more
nodes.evidence: a measured table: whole-file paste vs graph slice, tokens spent, answer quality, on three real questions.
nodes.why: Tokenomics as engineering instead of vibes. The graph computes the minimal context for a question; you measure what that is worth in money and accuracy.
nodes.reading: Module 09. Same doctrine as routing training, taught from the other side.
nodes.reviewFor: A measured pack: tokens and answer quality, whole-file paste versus graph slice.

tasks.title: nanograph pack --budget
tasks.done_when: Given a question and a token budget, the tool assembles the slice and the prompt.
how: Blast radius picks candidates; the budget trims them.

tasks.title: Measure it honestly
tasks.done_when: A committed table (or gist) in your nanograph repo includes at least one case where the slice LOST, plus why.
how: A benchmark with no losses is marketing, not measurement.
Done when the table lives in the repo or a stranger-openable URL, not only in chat.

nodes.title: Make it yours
nodes.evidence: your shipped fork: README with real numbers from a repo you care about, plus one analysis nobody asked for.
nodes.why: The finale is a fork, not a finish. This is the portfolio artifact that keeps working for you after the cohort, and the thing your defense can draw on.
nodes.reading: Modules 10-11. Full ceremony: contract, failure log, written review.
nodes.reviewFor: A shipped fork plus one analysis that exists only because you wanted the answer.

tasks.title: Ship the fork
tasks.done_when: A stranger can install it, run it on their repo, and read your numbers in the README.
how: Packaging is respect for the reader. Module 10.

tasks.title: One analysis nobody asked for
tasks.done_when: A query or view that exists because YOU wanted it, defended in one paragraph.
how: This is the part that gets reviewed hardest.

weekly.title: Ship one thing with a URL
weekly.done_when: A link posted in #ship from the last seven days.

weekly.title: One Coach session
weekly.done_when: You saved the review block and pasted it into #asks.
